replies.user: [CURRICULUM: Unit 1, Lesson 1] Teach me what physically happens inside an LLM when I type a prompt. Start with tokenization and next-token prediction. After explaining, give me a hands-on exercise.
replies.raw:
Here's something that might surprise you: the word "bank" is the **same token** whether you're talking about a riverbank or a savings account.

The model doesn't know which one you mean — not yet.

So how does it figure it out? That's exactly what this lesson is about.

---

Let's start at the very beginning: what happens the instant you hit send.

Your prompt doesn't enter the model as words. It gets sliced into **tokens** — chunks that are roughly (but not exactly) words. "Tokenization" is just a fancy name for that slicing step.

[KEY]Before an LLM reads a single word, it converts your text into tokens — small chunks that get turned into numbers the model can do math on.[/KEY]

[EX]GPT-4's tokenizer has a vocabulary of about 100,000 tokens. A word like "running" might be one token; an unusual word like "tokenization" might be split into two or three pieces.[/EX]

Those number-coded tokens are what actually travel into the model. The words you typed are already gone at this point — replaced by IDs.

[Q]
What does tokenization do to your prompt before the model processes it?
A) It searches the internet for relevant information about your words
B) It breaks your text into chunks and converts them into numbers
C) It checks your spelling and corrects any errors
ANS: B
[/Q]

replies.user: I picked B) It breaks your text into chunks and converts them into numbers
replies.raw:
Exactly right — the words become numbers before the model ever "thinks" about them.

Now here's where it gets interesting: remember that "bank" problem from the hook? Once your prompt is tokenized, the model needs to figure out which meaning applies. That's the job of the **attention mechanism**.

Attention lets every token "look at" every other token in your prompt and decide which ones matter most for understanding it.

[KEY]Attention is how the model resolves ambiguity — it weighs relationships between tokens so that context shapes meaning.[/KEY]

[EX]In "I sat on the bank of the river," the token "bank" pays high attention to "river" — that connection is what steers the model toward riverbank, not finance. On its own, "I went to the bank" is genuinely ambiguous; the surrounding words don't decide it.[/EX]

This happens across every token simultaneously, in layers, before the model produces a single word of output.

[Q]
In the sentence "I put cash in the bank," what does the attention mechanism use to figure out that "bank" means a financial institution?
A) It looks up "bank" in a built-in dictionary of word meanings
B) It notices the relationship between "bank" and "cash" in the same sentence
C) It memorized that "bank" usually means finance because that word appears more often online
ANS: B
[/Q]

replies.user: I picked C) It memorized that "bank" usually means finance because that word appears more often online
replies.raw:
Close, but not quite — and the distinction really matters.

Memorizing a word's *most common* meaning would mean "bank" always points to finance, no matter what surrounds it. But that's exactly what attention fixes: it reads the *specific context* of this sentence, right now. Put "river" nearby and the answer flips.

Put "cash" nearby and it flips back.

It's not about which meaning is more popular globally — it's about which neighboring tokens are pulling hardest in *this* prompt.

[Q]
In the sentence "I put cash in the bank," what does the attention mechanism use to figure out that "bank" means a financial institution?
A) It looks up "bank" in a built-in dictionary of word meanings
B) It notices the relationship between "bank" and "cash" in the same sentence
C) It memorized that "bank" usually means finance because that word appears more often online
ANS: B
[/Q]

replies.user: I picked B) It notices the relationship between "bank" and "cash" in the same sentence
replies.raw:
Yes — the local relationship between tokens is what does the work, not a global popularity contest.

Now for the final piece: what does the model actually *do* with all that context?

After attention has sorted out relationships between tokens, the model makes a prediction. Specifically, it predicts the **next token** — one at a time, over and over, until the response is complete.

It's not retrieving a stored answer. It's calculating: *given everything before this point, what token is most likely to come next?*

[KEY]An LLM generates output by predicting one token at a time — each new token is chosen based on all the tokens that came before it.[/KEY]

[EX]Given the prompt "The cat sat on the ___," the model assigns high probability to tokens like "mat" or "floor" and low probability to tokens like "democracy" — because the context strongly constrains what fits.[/EX]

Sometimes one continuation dominates and the model is very confident. Sometimes many continuations are equally plausible and confidence is spread thin.

That difference — high confidence vs. low confidence — is exactly what your exercise is about.

---

Now let's put this to work. Here's your exercise:

Read this sentence carefully:

*"After years of study, the scientist finally published her ___."*

1. Pick **one slot** where you think the model would predict with **high confidence**, and explain why.
2.

Pick **one slot** where you think the model would predict with **low confidence**, and explain why.

(The blank counts as a slot — but so do the other words in the sentence if you think any of them would be predicted differently.)

replies.user: For the exercise, concretely: the model is most confident at the end of a strong collocation — the slot where one continuation dominates training text. It's least confident at an open slot where several continuations are all plausible. Strong learned pattern → high confidence; open choice → low confidence.

replies.user: [CURRICULUM: Unit 1, Lesson 1] Teach me what physically happens inside an LLM when I type a prompt. Start with tokenization and next-token prediction. After explaining, give me a hands-on exercise.
replies.raw:
Here's something that might surprise you: an LLM never actually reads your words.

It reads **numbers** — and the journey from your words to those numbers is where everything begins.

When you type a prompt, the very first thing that happens is your text gets sliced into chunks called *tokens*. A token is roughly a word or word-piece — "running" might stay as one token, or split into "run" + "ning," depending on the system.

[KEY]Tokenization converts your text into numbered chunks before the model ever "sees" it.[/KEY]

[EX]GPT-4's tokenizer knows about 100,000 different tokens. Each one maps to a unique ID number — so your prompt becomes a list of integers, something like [15496, 11, 703, 527…], before any "thinking" happens.[/EX]

[Q]
What does a language model actually receive as input after you type your prompt?
A) Your original words, read left to right like a human would
B) A list of numbers representing chunks of your text
C) A search query sent to a database of pre-written answers
ANS: B
[/Q]

replies.user: I picked B) A list of numbers representing chunks of your text
replies.raw:
Exactly right — the model never touches your raw words, only those number sequences.

Now here's where it gets interesting. Once your prompt is a list of numbers, the model has to figure out what those numbers *mean* — and meaning is slippery.

Take the word "bank." It gets the same token whether you mean a riverbank or a financial institution. So how does the model sort that out?

This is where the **attention mechanism** comes in. It lets every token "look at" every other token in your prompt and decide which ones matter most for understanding it.

[KEY]Attention lets the model weigh relationships between tokens — so context, not just the word itself, determines meaning.[/KEY]

[EX]In "I sat on the bank of the river," the model's attention connects "bank" strongly to "river," pulling it toward the nature meaning. In "I put cash in the bank," attention connects it to "cash" instead. The sentence "I went to the bank" — with no such clues — stays genuinely ambiguous.[/EX]

[Q]
Why can't the model figure out what "bank" means just by looking at that one token alone?
A) Because "bank" is too short a word to carry meaning
B) Because the token ID number for "bank" doesn't encode which sense is intended
C) Because the model hasn't been trained on sentences with the word "bank"
ANS: B
[/Q]

replies.user: I picked C) Because the model hasn't been trained on sentences with the word "bank"
replies.raw:
Actually, that's the opposite of the situation — "bank" is one of the most common words in English, so the model has seen it countless times in training.

The real issue is that seeing it a million times doesn't help *in the moment* — because the same token ID gets used for both meanings every single time. The number itself carries no hint of which sense is meant.

That's exactly why attention exists: to pull meaning from the *surrounding* tokens, not from the word in isolation.

[Q]
Why can't the model figure out what "bank" means just by looking at that one token alone?
A) Because "bank" is too short a word to carry meaning
B) Because the token ID number for "bank" doesn't encode which sense is intended
C) Because the model hasn't been trained on sentences with the word "bank"
ANS: B
[/Q]

replies.user: I picked B) Because the token ID number for "bank" doesn't encode which sense is intended
replies.raw:
You got it — the number is just a label, and labels don't carry context. That's attention's whole job.

Now let's get to what the model actually *does* with all of this — because attention isn't the destination, it's the setup.

After processing your tokens through many layers of attention, the model arrives at one task: **next-token prediction**. It looks at everything before a blank and asks — what number (token) most plausibly comes next?

[KEY]An LLM generates text by predicting one token at a time, over and over, based on everything that came before.[/KEY]

[EX]Give it "The cat sat on the ___" and the model assigns high probability to tokens like "mat," "floor," "couch" — and near-zero probability to tokens like "democracy" or "seventeen." It picks from that distribution, outputs one token, then repeats the whole process.[/EX]

So the model isn't reading English. It's doing math on a sequence of integers.

[Q]
What does a tokenizer actually hand off to the rest of the model?

replies.user: I picked B) A list of numbers representing chunks of your text
replies.raw:
Exactly right — the words are gone at that point, replaced entirely by numbers.

Now here's where it gets interesting. A list of numbers doesn't carry *meaning* yet — "bank" in "river bank" and "bank" in "savings bank" might get the same token ID. Something has to sort that out.

That's where the **attention mechanism** comes in. The model looks at every token in relation to every other token, weighing which ones matter most for understanding each word in context.

[KEY]Attention lets the model figure out that "bank" means money when "cash" is nearby, and means riverbank when "river" is nearby.[/KEY]

[EX]Take the sentence "I went to the bank." On its own, that's genuinely ambiguous — "went," "to," and "the" don't decide it. But in "I put cash in the bank," attention pulls hard toward "cash," and the meaning locks in.[/EX]

The model doesn't look words up in a dictionary. It builds meaning from relationships between tokens, every single time.

[Q]
Why can the same token mean different things in different sentences?
A) The tokenizer assigns different ID numbers depending on context
B) The model looks up the word's definition in a built-in dictionary
C) The attention mechanism weighs nearby tokens to shape each token's meaning
ANS: C
[/Q]

replies.user: I picked A) The tokenizer assigns different ID numbers depending on context
replies.raw:
Actually, that's the one thing the tokenizer *doesn't* do — it assigns the same ID to "bank" every single time, no matter what's around it.

The tokenizer is just a lookup table. It's mechanical, context-blind, done before any understanding happens.

The meaning problem gets solved *later*, by attention — which is precisely why attention exists. Without it, the model would have no way to tell a river from a savings account.

[Q]
Why can the same token mean different things in different sentences?
A) The tokenizer assigns different ID numbers depending on context
B) The model looks up the word's definition in a built-in dictionary
C) The attention mechanism weighs nearby tokens to shape each token's meaning
ANS: C
[/Q]

replies.user: I picked C) The attention mechanism weighs nearby tokens to shape each token's meaning
replies.raw:
You got it — attention is what turns a context-blind number into something meaningful.

Now for the final piece: what does the model actually *do* with all that context it's built up?

It predicts the next token. That's it. That's the whole trick.

**Next-token prediction** means the model outputs a probability distribution over its entire vocabulary — every one of those ~100,000 tokens gets a score — and the highest-scoring one gets picked and added to the response. Then the process repeats, one token at a time.

[KEY]An LLM generates text by repeatedly asking "given everything so far, what token comes next?" — never planning the whole sentence at once.[/KEY]

[EX]Give a model the prompt "The cat sat on the ___" and it will assign very high probability to "mat," "floor," "couch" — and near-zero probability to "democracy" or "seventeen." The completion is almost locked in.[/EX]

Some slots are predictable; others are wide open. That difference matters a lot for understanding when AI is reliable and when it isn't.

[Q]
What does the model output at each step of generation?
A) The single correct next word, retrieved from a database
B) A probability score for every possible next token, then picks the top one
C) A complete sentence planned out in advance, then printed word by word
ANS: B
[/Q]

replies.user: For the exercise, concretely: the model is most confident at the end of a strong collocation — the slot where one continuation dominates training text. It's least confident at an open slot where several continuations are all plausible. Strong learned pattern → high confidence; open choice → low confidence.
replies.raw:
That's a sharp way to put it — and exactly right. Strong learned pattern → high confidence; open choice → low confidence.
